posts.content_md:
Hey John, a long time ago you linked to these neutral density filters, and mentioned that you have one:

[http://www.surplusshed.com/pages/item/m2611.html](http://www.surplusshed.com/pages/item/m2611.html) 

I was thinking of using these to annenuate beams from two of my lasers (100mW at 532nm and 205mW at 458nm). I was wondering if this is below the damage threshold, and what power/wavelength combinations you've used with yours. Thanks in advance, Joe

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Hey Joe, I did actually use it as an attenuator a few times. Here are my table geometries (can't believe I had these already illustrated).

The first one, does not take into account coherence length as I have so much and never worry about it ( I know I am spoiled). This is top view and using side beam reference beams. This is an H2 set up.

[http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/H2SetUp.jpg](http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/H2SetUp.jpg)

This one is only an illustration of how the geometry can be modified if one has shorter coherence length. I did not actually use this geometry. Again an H2 set up.

[http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustration ... erence.jpg](http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/H2SetUpCoherence.jpg)

This one, and I have used it, is the same as #1 above except I inserted a beam splitter and a few of mirrors to steal some light for illuminating an object in and H1 set up. This geometry allow H1 copy from an object and H2 copy from the H1 without redoing the table. Simply place the first beam splitter in the path, allign mirrors and spatial filter for object illumination, card off the H2 reference and shoot your H1. The attenuator is not shown here but I used it for the next step. Simply drop out the beam splitter and your are ready to go for the H2 copy.

[http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/H2SetUpWH1.jpg](http://www.holograms3d.com/Illustrations/H2SetUpWH1.jpg)

It really worked quite well and I was very please to be able to control the light ratios in a very simple H1 to H2 copy geometry.

So back to your question, I tried using this attenuator as a beam splitter in the raw beam but never liked the beams no matter what angle I tried. I did not see any damage on the attenuator using about (from memory) ~100mw at 488 and 514. I rarely crank it any higher for setting up the table. So I am pretty sure you will be ok, at least with 532. With that in mind and the fact they are cheap enough, you could buy one and do a little testing on it to make sure. Again I think you will be ok, but I didn't test it thouroughly enough.

If you want I can blast 500 or 600mw through it at 488 and 514 for 15 minutes each and see what happens.

posts.author: wler
posts.content_md: I have a variable circular ND filter I had used as a beam splitter and at numerous occasions had punched little irregularities in the metallic coating, in the order of 100-200mW at 514nm. You won't easily see them but the transmitted intensity then jumps at these spots, which makes adjustment sometimes a pain. In the end I switched to waveplates and pol. cubes, which has numerous advantages.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
wler, that is good information. The more information that is gathered on a subject the more accurate it becomes.

I set the attenuator up at a 45degree angle to reflect the beam 90 degrees. The attenuator was about 6 inches from my argon ion laser. Of couse I tred this about 5mm from the edge of the attenuator in case it did do damage it would be very near the edge. I dialed in 488 and cranked it up to 400mW. I left it there for 15 minutes while observing the reflected beam and the transmitted beam. The reflected beam was raw and I noticed nothing funning going on with it. Since this attenuator was plated in the beam path prior to my single beam reflection set up, I could monitor the transmitted beam via the single beam set up. I placed a white card where the plate goes and tweaked in my spatial filter after placing the attenuator in the beam path. I then monitored visually the transmitted beam, which again was an expanded, spatially filtered reference beam in a single beam set up. I noticed no deformation or intesity changes, but this was all done visually. I thought if something happened I would be able to see it. I did that same test for 514 at 300mW. And saw no adverse effects. I then manually visually inspected the attenuator in a nice bright light and saw no damage.

So, why the different findings? Of course the ND filter you used and the one I tested on could be coated differently. It could be that I did not let the laser cook the filter long enough and with longer times the filter may degrade. It could be the damage was so slight in 15 minutes that it was not observable easily. Not sure at this point but it does make me want to do more testing or closer observations.

I would have surely thought that 400mW would do something visually apparent realizing what Ed W. mentioned in another thread about the 100mW limit. I know I can only keep the back of my hand in the beam for about 5 seconds.

I will look at the spots I cooked under a microscope this evening. 

Joe, I would apreciate if you kept us posted when you get yours. These may be pretty good attenuators designed for some reason for higher powers. It seems wler and Ed W. both seem to observe damage at 100mW on filters they used.

posts.author: wler
posts.content_md:
I guess much depends on the coating, in fact there are several types. One thing I noticed, once I got suspicious, that the wheel I got absorbs quite a lot rather than reflects, which is bad since I wanted to use it as a variable splitter (and who has laser power to waste, eh?). I measured it once carefully, and I don't remember the result and the conditions any more, but roughly the losses were like 40-50% (adding reflected and transmitted powers). This means that a large portion of the power is absorbed in a small region, in the order of 1mm^2 within a very thin film, so no surprise that this causes damage. When running at high powers, like 250mW, I noticed even a moving pattern on the wall from reflections of the splitter.... that was the end of its use by me 

And apart from the damage, also thermal expansion effects can be harmful for holography. So my few cents would be to avoid all absorbing/dissipating optics.

I noticed surprisingly large losses in plenty of other things too, like cube splitters and metallic mirrors. In a mildly complicated setup one can easily loose 50% of the light in this way. Best thing is using AR coated waveplates and dielectric cubes, this can give just a few % losses.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: In my case, I'm just interested in attenuating the beam to reduce power. I'm planning to combine red, green, and blue, and need a way to vary the intensity of the green and blue (downward) for correct color balance. If John's attenuator can take it, so far it looks like the most attractive option, due to the low price. Another option would be to use the Edmund rectangular variable beamsplitter, which costs $79 (it would also be necessary to buy or build a mount for this). Variable attenuators can get surprisingly expensive, maybe it depends on the quality of the coating.
